matching.reasoningTemplate: Progressive headache with focal signs or new seizures raises concern for an intracranial mass.

clinicalPearls: Presenting features split into general (raised-ICP) symptoms - headache +/- nausea/vomiting, cognitive change, personality change, gait disorder - and focal/lateralizing signs such as hemiparesis, aphasia or visual field loss; many patients have both (p.716).

The classic morning-predominant headache that eases through the day occurs in only a minority of patients; brain-tumour headache is more often a nondescript dull ache, and migraine produces this pattern far more often than tumour (p.716, p.157).
Vomiting preceding headache by weeks is highly characteristic of posterior fossa tumours, and headache disturbs sleep in about 10% (p.157).
Seizures from a brain tumour always have a focal onset whether or not this is clinically apparent (p.716).
New de novo headache in a patient with known malignancy should raise suspicion of cerebral metastases or carcinomatous (leptomeningeal) meningitis (p.157).

On MRI, malignant tumours (primary or metastatic) typically enhance with gadolinium, have central necrosis and surrounding white-matter edema, whereas low-grade gliomas usually do NOT enhance and are best seen as increased signal on FLAIR (p.716).
Meningiomas and vestibular schwannomas are extra-axial, densely enhancing lesions; a meningioma characteristically shows a dural tail and compresses but does not invade brain (p.716, p.721).

Leptomeningeal disease produces multilevel neuraxis signs (radiculopathies, cranial neuropathies, seizures, confusion, raised-ICP encephalopathy); isolated focal deficits like hemiparesis are rarely from it unless brain is directly infiltrated (p.724).
Parinaud's syndrome (impaired upgaze and accommodation) points to a pineal-region mass (p.720).
harrison.pathophysiology: General/raised-ICP symptoms arise as the enlarging tumour plus surrounding vasogenic edema raises intracranial pressure or obstructs CSF circulation, producing hydrocephalus; focal deficits reflect local invasion or compression (p.716). Primary tumours develop through stepwise acquisition of genetic changes - loss of tumour-suppressor genes (p53, CDKN2A/B, PTEN) and amplification/overexpression of oncogenes such as EGFR and PDGFR - and glioblastomas in particular show marked molecular heterogeneity (p.717). The 2021 WHO CNS classification integrates molecular markers (e.g. IDH mutation, 1p/19q co-deletion) with histology into the diagnosis (p.717-718). Brain metastases spread hematogenously, lodging in terminal arterioles at the grey-white junction in watershed territory, so distribution follows blood flow (~85% supratentorial, ~15% posterior fossa) (p.723).
additionalDifferentials: Metastatic brain tumour - three times more common than all primary brain tumours combined in adults; commonest sources lung and breast, with melanoma having the greatest propensity to metastasize to brain (p.716, p.723)
Diffuse glioma - the most common malignant PRIMARY brain tumour; subdivided into IDH-mutant astrocytoma, IDH-mutant 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma, and IDH wild-type glioblastoma (p.717-718)
Meningioma - now the most common primary brain tumour overall (~35%); extra-axial dural-based lesion, WHO grades I-III (p.720-721)
Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) - ~9% of primary brain tumours, presents with progressive unilateral hearing loss/tinnitus/dizziness (p.721)
Primary CNS lymphoma - densely enhancing, often periventricular/basal ganglia/corpus callosum; associated with immunosuppression and EBV in HIV (p.720)
Pituitary adenoma - amenorrhoea/galactorrhoea with headache suggests a prolactinoma (p.157, p.721)
Pineal-region tumour presenting with Parinaud's syndrome and hydrocephalus (p.720)
Colloid cyst of the third ventricle - intermittent hydrocephalus, rarely sudden death (p.722)
infectionMimics: Brain abscess - shares a ring-enhancing radiographic appearance with metastasis and high-grade glioma (p.723)
Cerebral toxoplasmosis - in immunocompromised patients, multiple ring-enhancing lesions can be hard to distinguish from PCNSL or metastases (p.721)
nonInfectiousMimics: Demyelinating lesion - can mimic the nonspecific appearance of a brain metastasis (p.723)
Neurosarcoidosis - listed among lesions resembling metastatic disease on imaging (p.723)
Radiation necrosis in a previously irradiated patient - mimics tumour and may need PET/MR perfusion to distinguish recurrence from treatment effect (p.716, p.723)
additionalInvestigations: MRI with gadolinium is the preferred test; CT only if MRI cannot be done (p.716)
Neuroimaging is often the only test needed to diagnose a brain tumour; laboratory tests are rarely useful (p.716)
FLAIR sequences to detect non-enhancing low-grade gliomas (p.716, p.718)
Functional MRI for presurgical mapping of eloquent cortex (p.716)
PET, MR perfusion and MR spectroscopy to assess metabolic activity and help separate tumour progression from radiation/treatment necrosis (p.716)
CSF cytology / flow cytometry when leptomeningeal involvement is suspected (gold standard but positive in only ~50% on first LP, still misses ~10% after three samples) (p.720, p.724)

Stereotactic biopsy for histologic diagnosis when imaging is insufficient; in suspected PCNSL withhold glucocorticoids until biopsy because they are cytolytic and can render tissue non-diagnostic (p.720)
HIV testing and body PET/CT, spine MRI, CSF and slit-lamp eye exam to stage suspected PCNSL (p.720-721)
Serum tumour markers (e.g. beta-hCG) occasionally elevated in metastatic disease (p.716)
redFlags: Progressive, subacute focal/lateralizing deficit (hemiparesis, aphasia, visual field loss) (p.716)
Morning-predominant headache or headache with raised-ICP features (nausea/vomiting, worse with exertion or position change) (p.716, p.157)
Vomiting preceding headache by weeks - suggests a posterior fossa mass (p.157)
New de novo headache in a patient with known systemic cancer (p.157)
Personality change/apathy that may be mistaken for depression (p.716)
harrison.prognosis: Outcome is tumour-specific. Low-grade (grade 2) IDH-mutant astrocytoma usually transforms to higher grade with median survival around 10 years; high-grade IDH-mutant astrocytoma roughly 3-9 years (p.718). Oligodendrogliomas (IDH-mutant, 1p/19q co-deleted) are more therapy-responsive with median survival in excess of 10 years (p.718). Glioblastoma (IDH wild-type) is the most common malignant primary tumour and invariably recurs; with standard combined therapy median survival is ~15-18 months and 5-year survival ~10%; adverse factors include older age, unmethylated MGMT promoter, poor performance status and unresectable tumour (p.718-719). Diffuse midline glioma H3K27-altered carries a poor prognosis (~1 year) regardless of grade (p.719). Pilocytic astrocytoma (grade 1) and completely resected meningiomas/ependymomas can be cured (p.719-721). Brain metastases treated with WBRT have median survival of only ~4-6 months, though SRS achieves local control in 80-90% and occasional cure (p.724).
pitfalls: A ring-enhancing lesion is non-specific - the differential includes brain abscess, toxoplasmosis, PCNSL, demyelination, sarcoidosis, radiation necrosis and primary brain tumour, so do not assume tumour without context (p.721, p.723).

Withholding the diagnosis of glioma can be hard for diffusely infiltrative non-enhancing tumours (formerly gliomatosis cerebri), which often present only with cognitive decline and confluent FLAIR signal without mass effect (p.718).
Do not give glucocorticoids before biopsy in suspected PCNSL - their cytolytic effect can yield non-diagnostic tissue (p.720).
Prophylactic antiepileptic drugs have no role in tumour patients who have not had a seizure (only perioperative use is sometimes appropriate) (p.716).
A normal or migrainous headache pattern is far more often migraine than tumour - tumour headache is frequently nondescript (p.157).
Imaging-negative leptomeningeal disease is common; a single negative CSF cytology does not exclude it (positive in only ~50% on first LP) (p.724).
harrison.severityClassification: WHO CNS grading (2021 integrated histologic + molecular classification): diffuse gliomas graded 2-4 by histologic malignancy and molecular markers, with CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion conferring grade 4 to otherwise lower-grade IDH-mutant astrocytomas; pilocytic astrocytoma is grade 1. Meningiomas are graded I (benign), II (atypical) and III (malignant) by increasing aggressiveness (p.717-718, p.720-721).
